questions: Do you feel an irresistible urge to move your legs before these movements occur?
Are you aware of the movements while they are happening?
Can you briefly suppress the movements when you try?
Do the movements stop completely when you are asleep?
Do you have weakness or loss of sensation in either leg?
Have you recently started or increased a medication, especially an antipsychotic, anti-nausea drug, antidepressant, or seizure medication?
Have you had a recent stroke, head injury, infection, or other brain illness?
Do the movements occur continuously while you are awake, rather than in brief attacks?
Are both legs involved in a regular alternating “bicycling” or stepping pattern?
Do the movements become stronger when someone touches or moves your legs?
Do the movements occur when you are fully asleep?
Do you lose awareness or become confused during any episode?
Do you bite your tongue or lose bladder control during the movements?
Are the movements painful or associated with muscle cramps?
Do the movements occur only when you are lying in bed or resting?
Do they stop when you stand up or walk?
Is each movement sudden and brief, like a jerk, rather than a sustained posture?
Are the movements regular and repetitive at a steady rhythm?
Do the movements mainly affect one leg at a time?
Do the movements occur more often when you are drowsy or falling asleep?
Have these movements been present for more than one month?
Did these movements begin suddenly, within hours or a few days?
Do the movements vary substantially in speed, amplitude, or pattern from one episode to another?
Do the movements lessen or stop when you are distracted by a mental task, conversation, or voluntary movement of another body part?
Can you voluntarily reproduce a similar movement when asked?
Do the movements change or stop when you walk backward, perform a tandem gait, or keep a steady rhythm with your hands?
Have you had significant stress, anxiety, trauma, or a new interpersonal or occupational problem around the time these movements began?
Do you have movements in your arms, face, or trunk as well as your legs?
Do you have a history of diabetes mellitus or recently elevated blood glucose before this admission?
Did the movements begin after a sudden episode of facial drooping, speech difficulty, visual loss, or unilateral weakness?
Do you have hypertension, atrial fibrillation, high cholesterol, or a previous stroke?
Have you ever had similar involuntary movements in the past?
Do close relatives have Huntington disease or unexplained progressive chorea?
Do you have a malar rash, photosensitivity, joint inflammation, blood clots, recurrent miscarriages, or other autoimmune symptoms?
Have you taken dopamine-blocking or dopaminergic drugs at any time in the months before onset, even if not recently started or increased?
Have you previously had a confirmed stroke, even if it caused no lasting symptoms?
Do you currently have atrial fibrillation or another irregular heart rhythm?
Did the involuntary movements begin suddenly, or did they develop gradually over days to weeks?
Are the movements confined to the right side, with no abnormal movements on the left?
Do you have a history of cancer, HIV, syphilis, or other significant infection?
orders: Bedside neurological examination assessing muscle tone, reflexes, coordination, and whether the involuntary movements are choreiform, dystonic, or myoclonic
Electroencephalogram (EEG) with simultaneous video recording during a typical episode
Serum glucose, calcium, magnesium, sodium, potassium, renal function, liver function, and thyroid-stimulating hormone
MRI brain with T2/FLAIR, susceptibility-weighted imaging, and thin-section imaging of the basal ganglia and subthalamic nuclei
CT angiography or MR angiography of the head and neck
Transthoracic echocardiography and 12-lead ECG with rhythm monitoring to assess atrial fibrillation and cardiac embolic source
12-lead ECG and continuous inpatient telemetry monitoring for atrial fibrillation
Transthoracic echocardiography with contrast to assess for intracardiac thrombus or another cardioembolic source
Repeat MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging in 24–48 hours, focusing on the left basal ganglia and subthalamic region
served: deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses
